messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Elias Vance was forty-five when the hurricane-force winds and rising water collapsed the field hospital where he served as a military medic. He remembered the exact moment the canvas walls tore open, not as a single picture, but as a suffocating rush of debris, the deafening roar of water, and the frantic, failing triage of men pinned under twisted support beams. For weeks afterward, the silence of his suburban home felt wrong. Even when he knew he was safe, he could not relax, his muscles permanently coiled as if another collapse were imminent. The environment of his daily life had shifted from a place of service to a landscape of potential failure, and he began to treat every routine moment like a fragile perimeter. His body never stopped scanning the aisles of the military medical supply depot where he continued to work. He stood superalert and watchful, his eyes darting to the ceiling whenever a shelving unit groaned or a forklift backfired. He became intolerant of unexpected or loud sounds, flinching violently when a heavy crate dropped on the concrete floor or when a pressure valve hissed during inspection. Over months, this relentless state of being on guard slowly eroded the architecture of his former life. Because his nervous system refused to accept that the storm had passed, his shattered beliefs about how the world works took root. He began to see his deployments not as tragedies to be processed, but as proof that the fundamental rules of safety had been completely destroyed, leaving him with a profound sense of lost meaning. The memories did not arrive as coherent stories. When the event returned, Elias found he could not put the memories of the event in the right order, the images jumping between collapsed stretchers, screaming patients, and the dark water rising past his boots. He would sit at his kitchen table until the overwhelm on recall became too much, feeling so flooded by emotion that he had to stop and leave the room. Yet, each time the memories intruded, they actively dismantled his sense of self. The terror on recall, stripped of any protective context, fed directly into his negative appraisals. He would look in the mirror and feel like he didn't know himself anymore, certain that the man who had once cared for others was now just a hollow shell watching his own life slip away. The way he viewed his present reality dictated how the past continued to invade his days. His lost meaning and identity loss acted like a dark lens, warping how he accessed the event. Because he had come to believe that nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore and that his own moral compass had been obliterated, the trauma memories surfaced with intensified ferocity. His shattered beliefs stripped the memories of any therapeutic distance, pulling the terror on recall forward with violent urgency. Every time he tried to ground himself, the conviction that his beliefs about how the world works had been completely destroyed ensured that the memories returned not as recollections, but as immediate, inescapable threats. He had stopped entering the depot’s loading bay, unable to face the rolling crates of oxygen tanks or the sharp whine of pneumatic doors. His wife had died two years prior to the storm, and his isolation had deepened into a rigid routine of staying indoors, curtains drawn, listening to the rhythmic click of a ceiling fan just to mask the silence. The consequences were concrete: he could no longer sit through veteran gatherings, and the constant inability to relax meant he slept in twenty-minute increments. Finally, after a panic attack while watching a storm tracker on television, he scheduled an appointment with a trauma specialist. He was most afraid of what the therapist might ask him to remember, yet he hoped, against all his new convictions, that someone might help him untangle the loop keeping him trapped.
